qs.q: A 68-year-old man with resistant hypertension is evaluated for an add-on therapy that blocks mineralocorticoid receptors in the distal nephron. Which drug is a common fourth-line choice for resistant hypertension and has potential endocrine adverse effects such as gynaecomastia?
qs.e: Spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist used as a fourth-line option for resistant hypertension, though it can cause gynaecomastia due to non-specific endocrine activity. Eplerenone is more selective and has fewer endocrine side effects.

qs.q: A 35-year-old man: infertility, gynaecomastia, small firm testes, 47,XXY karyotype, elevated FSH/LH, low testosterone. Diagnosis?
qs.e: Klinefelter (47,XXY): primary testicular failure → hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (high FSH/LH, low testosterone), small firm testes, azoospermia, gynaecomastia. Kallmann is hypogonadotropic with anosmia.

ai.title: Gynecomastia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Gynecomastia is benign male breast tissue proliferation caused by an altered estrogen‑to‑androgen ratio. Recognise the common tropical aetiologies, stage severity, and manage underlying causes before considering surgery.

sections.p: A palpable, symmetric enlargement of male breast tissue due to proliferation of glandular ducts and stroma, not just fat. Diagnosis requires clinical exam and exclusion of pseudo‑gynecomastia (fat).
b: Firm, rubbery tissue 1–2 cm diameter beneath the nipple‑areolar complex
Absence of skin changes, nipple discharge, or lymphadenopathy

sections.p: Use the Rohrlich (or Simon) grading: Grade I – mild enlargement, no skin excess; Grade II – moderate with some skin redundancy; Grade III – marked enlargement with excess skin.
b: Grade I: <2 cm tissue, no ptosis
Grade II: 2–5 cm, mild ptosis
Grade III: >5 cm, obvious ptosis

sections.p: Classify aetiologies into physiological, pharmacological, endocrine, and systemic. In low‑resource East African settings, the most frequent are:
b: Physiological puberty and ageing
HIV infection and antiretroviral therapy (especially efavirenz)
Tuberculosis treatment (rifampicin) and chronic liver disease (hepatitis B/C)
Spironolactone, anti‑androgens, and 5α‑reductase inhibitors (finasteride)
Herbal remedies containing phyto‑estrogens

sections.p: Young men notice a tender, firm lump under the areola that may become painless over weeks. Systemic signs point to an underlying disease.
b: Bilateral in >80 % of cases
Tenderness early, then firm non‑tender mass
Possible accompanying signs: jaundice, spider naevi, testicular atrophy

sections.p: When imaging is unavailable, rely on thorough physical exam and laboratory pattern to exclude malignancy.

t.b: Is androgen deficiency contributing? Low levels support endocrine or drug‑induced cause
Elevated estradiol indicates increased peripheral conversion or hepatic failure
Abnormalities suggest chronic liver disease as a driver
Positive result directs attention to ART‑related gynecomastia
Distinguishes glandular tissue from fat; rules out tumour
Hyperthyroidism can raise SHBG and cause gynecomastia

sections.p: Although usually benign, certain features demand urgent evaluation.
b: Unilateral hard mass, skin ulceration, or nipple discharge – suspect breast cancer
Rapid growth >6 months, weight loss, night sweats – consider lymphoma or TB
Severe pain, infection, or ulceration – risk of cellulitis

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; surgery is second‑line for persistent Grade II–III after 12 months of observation.
b: Stop or substitute offending drugs (e.g., replace spironolactone with eplerenone)
Treat chronic liver disease (antivirals for hepatitis B/C, abstain from alcohol)
Optimize HIV therapy – switch efavirenz if possible
Surgical options: subcutaneous mastectomy or liposuction for Grade III

sections.p: Re‑evaluate at 3‑month intervals after removing the trigger. Counsel on avoiding anabolic steroids and herbal estrogens.
b: Monitor hormone profile and liver tests every 6 months
Educate patients on signs of malignancy
Encourage weight control to reduce pseudo‑gynecomastia

sections.p: Distinguish true gynecomastia from conditions that mimic breast enlargement.
b: Pseudo‑gynecomastia – excess adipose tissue, no firm glandular core
Male breast carcinoma – usually unilateral, hard, fixed, may have skin retraction
Lipoma of the chest wall – soft, mobile, not centred under nipple

sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal despite pathology.
b: Normal total testosterone with low free testosterone in hepatic disease
Estradiol within reference range but high estrogen‑to‑androgen ratio due to low testosterone

faq.a: It blocks androgen receptors and increases estrogen activity, shifting the hormonal balance toward estrogen.

faq.q: Is breast cancer common in men with gynecomastia?
faq.a: Male breast cancer is rare (<1 % of cancers) but should be considered if the enlargement is unilateral, hard, or associated with skin changes.
Weight loss reduces pseudo‑gynecomastia (fat) but does not affect true glandular proliferation.

exam: What history points would make you suspect a drug‑induced cause? — Identify recent use of spironolactone, finasteride, antiretrovirals, or herbal supplements.
How would you differentiate true gynecomastia from pseudo‑gynecomastia on exam? — Palpate for firm sub‑areolar tissue versus diffuse soft fat.

A 17‑year‑old presents with bilateral breast enlargement and tenderness; labs show normal testosterone but elevated estradiol. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step? — Physiological pubertal gynecomastia; reassure and observe for 12 months.
In a patient with chronic hepatitis B and gynecomastia, which investigation is most informative? — Liver function tests and serum estradiol to assess hepatic estrogen metabolism.

Why is tamoxifen preferred over aromatase inhibitors for short‑term treatment? — Tamoxifen blocks estrogen receptors in breast tissue with fewer bone effects; aromatase inhibitors can worsen low testosterone.
What red‑flag feature would prompt urgent imaging? — Unilateral hard mass, skin ulceration, or nipple discharge suggesting malignancy.
Explain why 5α‑reductase inhibitors can cause gynecomastia. — They reduce conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, increasing the relative estrogen effect.
A patient on efavirenz develops gynecomastia; what management change would you consider? — Switch to an alternative ART regimen without efavirenz if virologically feasible.
